Phoenix by the numbers

Who sends the property tax bill in Phoenix?

Maricopa County does, not the city. The Maricopa County Assessor sets the value and classification of each parcel, and the Maricopa County Treasurer bills and collects the money. The Treasurer describes the job as collecting real and personal property taxes for more than 1,800 tax districts, including the state, the county, incorporated cities and towns, schools, community colleges and special districts, then passing the money on.

A Phoenix owner therefore has two offices to call, and each answers a different question.

  • Assessor: the value on your Notice of Valuation, the legal class of the home, appeals, notices of claim and personal exemptions. The office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, and the appeals line is 602-506-3406.
  • Treasurer: the amount due, payment options, refunds, delinquent notices and tax lien information.

The city of Phoenix sets its own rates, but it does not assess your home or collect from you. Its share arrives as one line on the county bill.

When are Phoenix property taxes due?

Half is due October 1 and half is due the next March 1, under A.R.S. 42-18052. Each half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 and May 1. If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

That rule matters this year. November 1, 2026 was a Sunday, so the Treasurer's calendar shows the first half of 2026 taxes becoming delinquent on Monday, November 2, after 5 p.m. As of November 15, an unpaid first half is already late. May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so the second-half deadline should roll to Monday, May 3, 2027.

Interest on late taxes runs at 16 percent per year simple, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month (A.R.S. 42-18053). The same statute says no interest is collected if the full-year tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year. For a 2026 bill with the first half unpaid, that gives you until Thursday, December 31, 2026 to pay both halves and avoid interest. Bills of $100 or less are due in one payment on October 1 and become delinquent after December 31.

How big is Phoenix, and what does that mean for a tax bill?

Phoenix is the capital of Arizona and the seat of Maricopa County. Wikipedia gives its area as about 518 square miles, the largest of any Arizona city, and the Census Bureau counted 1,665,481 residents in its July 2025 estimate. Settlers began farming the Salt River Valley in 1867, and the city was incorporated on February 25, 1881.

Size matters for taxes because a single city holds very different housing stock. The city organizes itself into 15 urban villages, including Ahwatukee Foothills, Camelback East, Laveen, Maryvale, Encanto and South Mountain. Homes in Maryvale and Ahwatukee Foothills sit under the same city, yet the school, community college and special districts on each bill depend on the parcel.

  • Census 2020 to 2024 figures for Phoenix: 57.3 percent owner-occupied housing, a median owner-occupied home value of $420,700, and median gross rent of $1,582.
  • Households total 610,442, with a median household income of $81,332.

Look up your parcel on the Assessor's site to see which taxing districts apply. Two houses a mile apart can have different total rates.

What does the city of Phoenix itself charge per $100 of value?

For 2026-27 the city's published notice proposed a primary rate of $1.2652 per $100 of assessed valuation, down slightly from $1.2658, and a secondary rate of $0.7745, down from $0.8141. The city said that although the primary rate was lower, rising assessed values would still raise primary taxes for the average owner by 2.79 percent. Its hearing was held June 17, 2026, so ask the Treasurer for the rates that were finally adopted.

Primary and secondary taxes pay for different things, according to the city's notice.

  • Primary tax supports General Fund services such as police and fire, parks and recreation, libraries and community centers. State law caps how fast a city's primary levy may grow (A.R.S. 42-17051).
  • Secondary tax pays bonded debt service for facilities like libraries, police and fire stations, storm drains and parks.

These are only the city's rates. Your county, school district and community college add their own, so your bill total is higher than the city line. Maricopa County posts the rate and levy tables for each taxing jurisdiction on its Tax Levy and Rates page.

How do you challenge a Phoenix home valuation?

File a petition with the Maricopa County Assessor within 60 days after the date the Notice of Valuation was mailed (A.R.S. 42-16051). For the notice mailed February 20, 2026, the Assessor's deadline was April 21, 2026, and that window has closed. Notices for the following cycle arrive in late winter, so check the mail date printed on yours and count 60 days from it.

The Assessor's appeals page separates three filings, and picking the wrong one wastes time.

  • Real property appeal: use it when you think the full cash value or classification is wrong. The Petition for Review of Valuation (AZDOR Form 82130R) can go in by mail or in person, and the office says emails are not accepted for real property appeals.
  • Notice of Claim: use it for a factual error such as wrong square footage. It covers the current year and the three prior years, and an approved claim can produce a refund through the Treasurer.
  • Residential Legal Class Change: use it when the home became your primary residence. A driver's license, voter registration, or a tax return address page plus a vehicle registration or utility bill must show your name and the property address.

Bring evidence to any of these. The Assessor says appeals without documents such as appraisals or comparable sales may be denied.

What tax relief can Phoenix homeowners apply for?

The Assessor's Valuation Relief division runs personal exemptions for widowed owners, totally disabled owners and veterans. Applications are due by February 28, or by September 1 with an approved Exemption Deadline Waiver. All programs require both Arizona residency and household income under the statutory limit.

  • Widowed or totally disabled: an exemption of up to $4,873 off the limited property value.
  • Veteran with a service-connected disability under 100 percent, or a nonservice-connected disability: up to $4,873, multiplied by the disability percentage.
  • Veteran with a 100 percent service-connected rating: the primary residence is fully exempt if all requirements, including income, are met.

The Assessor lists the income cap as $39,865 for households with no children under 18 and $47,826 where children under 18 or disabled children lived in the home during the prior year. Social Security, military pensions and veterans' disability payments are not counted as income. Call 602-506-3406 before you apply, since a purchase or sale of property can end eligibility.

What happens if you sell a Phoenix house with property tax unpaid?

Clear the unpaid tax before or at closing. A county treasurer can sell the tax lien for all delinquent taxes on a property together, and the sale is not limited to a single year (A.R.S. 42-18104). Ask your title company to pull the balance and show it on the settlement statement.

A few practical steps keep the closing on schedule.

  • Ask the title or escrow officer for a payoff figure that includes interest through the closing date.
  • If the first half of 2026 is still open, remember that interest is already running from November 2.
  • If you recently paid off a mortgage, ask the Treasurer about the interest waiver in A.R.S. 42-18053(C). It applies to a delinquency within one year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, needs board of supervisors approval, and can be used once per property.

The deed is recorded with the Maricopa County Recorder, which cannot give legal advice or help fill in documents and does not provide notary services. Its recording services line is 602-506-3535. This works the same whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan.

More questions about Phoenix, AZ Property Tax Guide

Does the city of Phoenix collect my property tax?

No. Maricopa County does. The Assessor sets the value and the Treasurer bills and collects, including the city's share. Phoenix sets its own rate, but it appears as one line on the county bill.

What is the deadline to pay 2026 Phoenix property tax without interest?

December 31, 2026 for the full year. Under A.R.S. 42-18053, no interest is collected if the full-year tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year. If you pay only the first half after its November 2 delinquency date, interest starts to run on the unpaid half.

What interest rate applies to late property tax in Maricopa County?

Sixteen percent per year, simple, from the delinquency date until paid. A fraction of a month counts as a whole month. State law lets the treasurer, with board approval, waive interest once per property for a delinquency within a year after a mortgage is released.

Can I still appeal my Phoenix home value for this cycle?

The window for the notice mailed February 20, 2026 closed on April 21, 2026. For the next notice, file within 60 days of its mail date. If you see a factual error such as wrong square footage, a Notice of Claim can still reach back three prior tax years.

Do I have to pay the tax before I can sell?

Clear it before or at closing, with interest included in the payoff. Ask the Maricopa County Treasurer or your title officer for the exact payoff for your parcel.

Tucson by the numbers

Who bills property tax in Tucson?

The Pima County Treasurer bills and collects property tax on a Tucson house, and the Pima County Assessor sets its value. The city's own levy is collected through that county statement.

Two offices handle most questions:

  • Pima County Assessor, 240 N. Stone Avenue, Tucson, AZ 85701, 520-724-8630: valuation, classification, notices of value, appeals and exemptions.
  • Pima County Treasurer, 520-724-8341: statements, payments, delinquency and lien redemption.

Tucson is the Pima County seat. The Census Bureau counts 228,020 households there for 2020 to 2024, with 51.8% owner-occupied, so just under half of households do not own their home. Owners of rentals and owner-occupants get the same county bill.

What are the Tucson property tax due dates for 2026 and 2027?

Pima County bills in two installments. The first is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1. The second is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1. When a delinquency date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to 5 p.m. the next business day.

Taxes of $100 or less are due in full in the first installment. If you have not paid the 2026 first half, call the Treasurer for the balance now due. First-half interest is waived only if the full year is paid or postmarked before 5 p.m. on December 31.

What is the Tucson city property tax rate?

The Tucson City Manager's April 21, 2026 recommended budget proposes a primary property tax rate of $0.4245 per $100 of assessed valuation for fiscal year 2027, which is $0.0208 below the FY26 rate. The drop comes mostly from a smaller tort liability claim in the levy, from $1,733,290 to $989,850.

The same memo projects primary property tax revenue of $20,777,930, with $19,788,080 going to the General Fund. The memo keeps the levy within 2% above the prior year's maximum allowable levy, plus new construction, as the state constitution allows.

The city's rate is only part of your bill. The Arizona Department of Revenue explains that tax equals assessed value times an overall rate set by the town or city, county, school and special districts. Your Pima County statement shows the combined rate that applies in your tax area.

How do I pay Pima County property tax, and what does it cost?

You can pay online, in person, by mail or by wire. The online portal takes most debit and credit cards, PayPal and eCheck, and charges a convenience fee.

  • eCheck: $0.50 per transaction.
  • Cards and other digital wallets online: 1.95% of the payment, with a $1.95 minimum.
  • In person at the Pima County Public Service Center: card, cash, check, cashier's check or money order, with a 2% fee on card payments.
  • By mail: check, cashier's check or money order in US funds payable to the Pima County Treasurer. Do not mail cash.
  • Returned items: $25.00 charge.

The Treasurer cautions that the post office does not always postmark mail, so mail early or get a receipt. Bank wires are arranged through the office at 520-724-8341. If a lender pays your taxes, ask them to confirm each payment. Change a mailing address through the Assessor, which requires a notarized form unless you update it online on the parcel record.

How do I appeal my Tucson property valuation?

File a petition with the Pima County Assessor within 60 days of the postmark on your Notice of Value. Those notices go out on or before March 1. An appeal challenges the valuation or classification, not the size of the tax bill.

Pima County lists four appeal tracks:

  • Petition: 60 days after a Notice of Value mailed on or before March 1.
  • Supplemental: 25 days after a Notice of Change mailed on or before September 30.
  • Notice of Proposed Correction: 60 days, when the Assessor starts a correction at any time of year.
  • Notice of Claim: an owner-started appeal for factual errors in the record.

You must name a valuation method. A market approach cites the sale price of at least one comparable property in the same area or a sale of your own property. Your case is stronger if the record has wrong details, if full cash value exceeds similar homes or sales in the last three years, or if the limited property value was calculated incorrectly.

The Assessor rules on all appeals by August 15. After that you can go to the State Board of Equalization within 25 calendar days of the decision, which must rule by October 15, and then to Tax Court within 60 days of the latest administrative decision. An owner who skipped the administrative route may go straight to Tax Court by December 15 of the valuation year.

Which exemptions and relief programs can lower a Tucson tax bill?

Arizona offers exemptions for veterans with disabilities, widows and widowers, and people with a total and permanent disability, plus a valuation freeze for seniors. The Pima County Assessor administers them, and the Valuation Relief Team can be reached at 520-724-7500 or ASRValRelief@pima.gov.

Key points from the Assessor and the Department of Revenue:

  • A 100% service-connected disabled veteran can receive an exemption on one primary residence, effective for tax year 2026 and after under H.B. 2792, signed February 12, 2026. The veteran must be honorably discharged, hold a VA benefit summary letter and meet income limits.
  • The income cap is $34,901 with no children under 18 at home, or $41,870 if a qualifying child lives there.
  • The Department of Revenue says new veteran exemption applications go to the Assessor between the first Monday in January and March 1.
  • The Senior Freeze, formally the Property Valuation Protection Option, fixes a primary residence's valuation for a renewable three-year period for owners who meet age and income limits.
  • Widow, widower and total and permanent disability exemptions cover a set dollar amount, with assessed value and income limits.

When a surviving spouse sells a home that carries the veteran's exemption, the exemption ends with the sale.

What happens to unpaid Tucson property tax when I sell?

Unpaid tax is settled from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask your title company to request a payoff figure from the Pima County Treasurer that matches the closing date, since interest may add to a past-due balance.

Pima County also allows a person who owns an interest in the property, an agent, an assignee or an attorney to redeem a sold tax lien in full, and any person may pay on the owner's behalf as a charitable gift. The Treasurer's office can tell you who qualifies to redeem and what proof is needed.

If you plan to sell to a cash buyer, tell them about any delinquent installment up front. A house with a past-due 2026 first half can still close, since escrow pays the balance and records the deed with an Affidavit of Property Value.

More questions about Tucson, AZ Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Tucson send a separate property tax bill?

No. The Pima County Treasurer bills all property tax, including the City of Tucson levy, on one statement. The City Manager's recommended FY27 primary rate was $0.4245 per $100 of assessed valuation.

When is the second half of Tucson property tax due?

March 1, 2027 is the due date, and it becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1. Pima County lists the postmark deadline for the 2026 second half as May 3, 2027.

What happens if I missed the November 2, 2026 deadline?

The first half is delinquent and interest applies. Paying the full year before 5 p.m. on December 31, 2026 waives interest on the first installment. Call the Treasurer at 520-724-8341 for the exact balance.

How do I appeal my Tucson property value?

File a petition with the Pima County Assessor within 60 days of the postmark on your Notice of Value, which is mailed on or before March 1. The Assessor must rule by August 15, and you have 25 calendar days after that decision to go to the State Board of Equalization.

Is there a property tax exemption for disabled veterans in Tucson?

Yes. A veteran with a 100% service-connected disability rating can apply to the Pima County Assessor for an exemption on one primary residence for tax year 2026 and later, subject to income limits. Call 520-724-7500 for the Valuation Relief Team.

Yuma by the numbers

Who bills property tax in Yuma, Arizona?

The Yuma County Treasurer bills and collects property tax for homes in the city of Yuma, and the Yuma County Assessor sets the values. Yuma is the county seat, so both offices work from 197 S. Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364. The Treasurer's counter is in Suite 203 of that building.

The Treasurer's page lists (928) 539-7781 and treasury@yumacountyaz.gov for questions. You can pay by scanning the QR code on your coupon, online at yumacountyaz.gov/paytaxes, by phone at 1-877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 1311, or by mailing a check or using bank bill pay to Yuma County Treasurer, 197 S. Main St., Suite 203. The page warns that 2024 delinquent taxes must be paid in certified funds.

For assessment questions, the Assessor's number is (928) 373-6040 and the email is assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov. Owner names, parcel details and sales data are on the Assessor's online records site, which replaced the old ITAX property tax site.

When are property taxes due in Yuma?

Yuma County follows the state schedule, so each half is due on the 1st of October and March and turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 and May 1. The Treasurer's calendar adjusts those dates when they land on a weekend, which explains the 2026 and 2027 dates below.

What does the City of Yuma add to the bill?

The city levies a primary property tax of its own, and it must announce increases in public. In a notice dated May 28, 2026, the City of Yuma said it proposed to raise primary property taxes by $431,353, or 2.51 percent, over the prior year. The notice, issued under A.R.S. 42-17107, said primary tax on a $100,000 home would come to $213.21 with the increase, against $207.99 without it.

The city scheduled the truth in taxation hearing for its June 17, 2026 council meeting at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall, One City Plaza, with the budget vote at the same meeting. The fiscal year 2027 budget totals about $570.8 million across all funds, and the June agenda also covered 13 Municipal Improvement Districts.

City Council meets on the first and third Wednesdays of the month at 5:30 p.m. in Council Chambers. Ask the Yuma County Treasurer for a line-by-line breakdown of the jurisdictions on your parcel, since the amount you owe depends on the district codes tied to the property.

How do you challenge a Yuma property valuation?

You file with the Assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Value was mailed. The card lists the exact deadline for the year. For the 2027 notices, the Assessor mailed them on February 20, 2026 and set an appeal date of April 20, 2026, which has passed, so the next notices will arrive in early 2027.

Before you appeal, read the Notice of Value closely. It lists Full Cash Value and Limited Property Value, and the back explains the legal class codes.

  • Code 3.01 means an owner-occupied primary residence. Owners with that code already receive the Less State Aid to Education reduction from the Treasurer.
  • Code 4.02 marks a rental. If the classification is wrong, the Assessor wants proof that you live in the home more than nine months a year.
  • Acceptable proof includes an Arizona driver's license, Arizona ID card, voter card or state income tax return, along with the Affidavit of Primary Residence.

The Assessor's legal calendar says appeals to tax court end on December 15. Unusually many 2027 notices came back as undeliverable, so call the office if yours never arrived.

What relief programs are open to Yuma homeowners?

Three programs show up on the county's pages, and all three run through the Assessor.

  • Widow, widower and disability exemption. It also covers churches and certain non-profit organizations. The filing period runs from the first working day in January to March 1, and the Assessor links the 2026 guidelines and a physician's Certification of Disability form.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection Option. Also called the Senior Freeze, it has a filing period from January 1 to September 1.
  • Veterans exemption. It falls under A.R.S. 42-11111, as changed by House Bill 4168. The Assessor says it takes effect for tax year 2027 and that applications open January 4, 2027, with a one-page flyer on the Assessor's page explaining who qualifies.

Bring identification and ask the Assessor what proof applies to your situation before you file.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens if you sell a Yuma house with tax still owed?

The unpaid tax stays attached to the house, and escrow normally pays it from the seller's proceeds. Under A.R.S. 42-17153, the tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year and outranks other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for taxes of other years. A buyer or lender will want it cleared.

Interest on late tax runs at 16 percent simple interest a year under A.R.S. 42-18053, with no interest if the full year is paid by December 31. The Treasurer's calendar also lists a 5 percent penalty on January 1, 2027 for delinquent 2025 taxes, followed by a tax lien sale in February. The 2026 sale took place February 17 at the Board of Supervisors Auditorium, 197 S Main St., with registration at 8:00 a.m. and bidding at 9:00 a.m.

Ask the Treasurer for a current payoff on your parcel before you sign a contract. Late years cost more each month, so the earlier you know the figure, the more room you have to negotiate.

What is Yuma like for a homeowner?

Yuma sits in the southwestern corner of Arizona on the Colorado River, close to the California line and Mexico. It became an incorporated town in 1902 and a city on April 7, 1914, and the 2020 census counted 95,548 residents. The Marine Corps Air Station and the Yuma Proving Ground anchor the local economy alongside winter vegetable farming.

The climate is hot desert. Yuma averages roughly 3 inches of rain a year and about 117 days at or above 100 degrees, which puts steady wear on roofs, cooling systems and exterior paint. Most of the city lies in the Yuma Union High School District, with central and eastern Yuma in Yuma Elementary District One and the northwest in the Crane district.

More questions about Yuma, AZ Property Tax Guide

When is Yuma property tax due?

Half is due October 1 and half March 1. The first half of 2026 taxes became delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026, and the second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 3, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest.

Who do I call about my Yuma property tax bill?

Call the Yuma County Treasurer at (928) 539-7781 or write to treasury@yumacountyaz.gov for billing and payment questions. For value and classification questions, call the Yuma County Assessor at (928) 373-6040 or email assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov. Both offices are at 197 S. Main Street in Yuma.

How long do I have to appeal my Yuma property value?

You have 60 days from the date the Notice of Value was mailed, and the card prints your deadline. For the 2027 notices that date was April 20, 2026, so it has passed. Tax court appeals must be filed by December 15, according to the Assessor's calendar.

Does the City of Yuma charge its own property tax?

Yes. The City of Yuma levies a primary property tax, and in May 2026 it proposed a 2.51 percent increase of $431,353, with a public hearing on June 17, 2026. Ask the Yuma County Treasurer for the jurisdiction breakdown on your parcel.

What penalty applies to late Yuma County property tax?

Interest is 16 percent simple per year from delinquency under A.R.S. 42-18053. The Treasurer's calendar also lists a 5 percent penalty on January 1, 2027 for delinquent 2025 taxes, followed by a tax lien sale on February 18, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest.

Cash Home Buyers in Arizona

  • Scottsdale, AZ Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Scottsdale, AZ Property Tax Guide sale

Scottsdale by the numbers

Who bills property tax for a house in Scottsdale, Arizona?

Scottsdale homeowners pay property tax to Maricopa County, not to the city office. The Maricopa County Assessor sets the value and the Maricopa County Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. The city of Scottsdale levies its own rate, which rides on the same county bill alongside the school district, fire and other districts that tax your parcel.

The city’s tax page lists the 2025/26 city property tax rate as $0.4891 primary and $0.4233 secondary, $0.9124 combined, per $100 of assessed valuation. The primary rate pays for general city operations. The secondary rate pays debt on voter-approved bonds. Rates for 2026/27 may differ, so read the rate lines on your own bill.

Scottsdale covers 184 square miles of land in eastern Maricopa County and has an estimated 243,006 residents as of July 1, 2025. It was named in 1894 for Winfield Scott, a retired Army chaplain, and incorporated on June 25, 1951. It borders Phoenix, Paradise Valley, Carefree, Fountain Hills and Tempe, along with the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community and Tonto National Forest, so a parcel near a boundary should be checked on the bill to confirm which city and districts it falls in.

When are Scottsdale property taxes due, and what is the next deadline?

The first half of the 2026 bill came due October 1 and became delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 2, 2026. The second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest on the first half. The Treasurer sends final delinquent notices on December 1 for unpaid 2025 taxes.

Bills of $100 or less become delinquent after 5 p.m. on December 31. Interest on late tax runs at 16 percent a year simple. The statute also lets the county treasurer, with board approval, waive interest and penalties on a delinquency within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust on the property is released, once per property, under ARS 42-18053.

What do the Scottsdale numbers look like?

These city figures come from Census QuickFacts.

  • Median owner-occupied home value of $789,800 for 2020 to 2024.
  • 67.0 percent of housing is owner-occupied, across 118,637 households.
  • Median household income of $110,886 and 2.03 persons per household.
  • 26.4 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 61.9 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor’s degree or higher.

A high assessed value does not mean a high bill. Taxes are computed on the limited property value, and a rise in that value is capped at 5 percent a year unless there is new construction, a significant change to the property or a change of use, according to the Assessor.

What neighborhoods and housing types affect Scottsdale tax bills?

The city is loosely split into South Scottsdale, Old Town, the central Shea Corridor and North Scottsdale. South Scottsdale, running north from McKellips Road toward Thomas Road, has long been the working-class part of the city and carries ASU’s SkySong research center. Old Town holds the downtown arts district and Scottsdale Fashion Square. The Shea Corridor has many houses from the 1970s plus master-planned communities such as Gainey Ranch and McCormick Ranch. North Scottsdale is the most actively developed area and holds many of the priciest homes in the state.

Part of north and east Scottsdale is protected: voters approved a sales tax in 1995 to buy land for the McDowell Sonoran Preserve, which is planned at 36,000 acres, nearly a third of the city’s land area. Work on the Indian Bend Wash Greenbelt, a 12-mile park corridor built for flood control, began in earnest after a 1972 flood and was completed in 1984. Owners near these areas should check parcel data for flood and preserve boundaries before listing.

The Scottsdale Airpark, around the city airport, is a major employment center in the north of the city. Desert heat matters for a house: the July daily mean maximum is 104.1 degrees F and annual rainfall is about 8.7 inches, so roofs, cooling systems and pool equipment draw attention in any inspection.

How do I appeal a Scottsdale property valuation?

File a Petition for Review of Valuation (Form 82130R for homes) with the Maricopa County Assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Value was mailed. Notices go out on or before March 1. The 2027 notice went out February 20, 2026, and its April 21, 2026 deadline has passed. The Assessor’s office is at 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, and the phone is 602-506-3406. Emails are not accepted for appeals, and an appeal without documents such as comparable sales or an appraisal may be denied.

You can appeal only the full cash value or the legal class, not the limited property value that sets your tax. The Assessor must answer by August 15. If you disagree, you have 25 days to go to the State Board of Equalization, which hears these appeals in Maricopa County and must issue decisions by mid-October. A court appeal, either tax court or small claims, is due by December 15 of the notice year, or within 60 days of the last administrative decision. Small claims can hear appeals on owner-occupied homes and on property valued under $2 million. The tax court line is 602-506-8297.

  • Use a Notice of Claim for a factual error such as wrong square footage or year built. It can reach the current year and the three tax years before it and may produce a refund.
  • Use the Residential Legal Class Change form if the house recently became your primary residence. A change made between January 1 and July 1 can fix both the current and next tax year.

What happens if Scottsdale property taxes go unpaid?

The Maricopa County Treasurer secures unpaid taxes by selling liens, as ARS 42-18101 directs, and sales run through an online auction vendor. The lien is a claim for the tax and the owner still holds the house, but it must be paid with interest to clear it. You can reach the Treasurer’s tax lien staff at 602-506-8511.

Short-term rentals add another layer. The city charges a 5.0 percent transient lodging tax on lodging for 29 days or less, on top of its 1.7 percent privilege tax. That is a separate tax from the property bill, but a house used for guests may also carry a different legal class on the county roll, so ask the Assessor how it is classified.

How should a Scottsdale seller deal with a tax bill?

  • Look up the parcel on the Treasurer’s site and write down every balance, including earlier years.
  • Call the Treasurer for a payoff that includes interest through the closing date.
  • Ask the Assessor about legal class, exemptions and the mailing address before the sale.
  • Give the payoff figures to the title or escrow company handling your closing.

Ask the Maricopa County Assessor which property tax exemptions apply to your situation. State law covers widows, widowers, people with a total and permanent disability, and disabled veterans under ARS 42-11111, and conveying title ends the exemption on the sold property.

More questions about Scottsdale, AZ Property Tax Guide

Who do I pay property tax to in Scottsdale?

You pay the Maricopa County Treasurer. The Maricopa County Assessor sets the value. The city of Scottsdale levies a rate, but its tax is collected on the county bill, so there is one bill and one payment.

When is the next Scottsdale property tax due date?

The second half of the current bill is due March 1, 2027 and is delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1, 2027. The first half was delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 2, 2026. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest on the first half.

What is the Scottsdale city property tax rate?

The city lists $0.4891 primary and $0.4233 secondary, $0.9124 combined, per $100 of assessed valuation for 2025/26. The 2026/27 figures may differ, and your bill also includes school, fire and county rates.

Can I still appeal my Scottsdale valuation this year?

Not for the 2027 notice, whose deadline of April 21, 2026 has passed. A Notice of Claim may still fix a factual error for the current year and three earlier years. The next appeal window opens when the Assessor mails notices by March 1.

Does a new owner in Scottsdale get a chance to appeal?

In some cases. The Assessor says a new owner of property whose value or class the former owner did not appeal may file in court before December 15 of the year the taxes are levied. The usual administrative deadline is 60 days after the Notice of Value is mailed.

Who sends the property tax bill for a house in Mesa, Arizona?

The Maricopa County Treasurer bills and collects it. The City of Mesa states that property taxes are billed by and paid to the Maricopa County Treasurer's Office, and the Maricopa County Assessor sets the value. The city does not assess or collect. A Mesa bill combines levies from the county, the school district, community college district, special districts and the city, all on one statement.

Mesa sits in Maricopa County and borders Tempe on the west, Chandler, Gilbert and Queen Creek on the south, Apache Junction on the east and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community on the north. For payment questions, call the Treasurer's customer service at 602-506-8511. For value questions, call the Assessor at 602-506-3406.

What city property tax does Mesa charge?

Mesa collects no primary property tax and does collect a secondary property tax. Under Arizona's two-part system, the city's secondary tax pays principal and interest on voter-approved general obligation bonds for libraries, parks and recreation, public safety and transportation.

The city also notes that Mesa has Community Facility Districts, where bonds were issued for property development and the cost is assessed to owners. Ask the Treasurer whether your parcel sits in one, since it adds to the bill.

When is Mesa property tax due?

Mesa follows the county calendar. Under A.R.S. 42-18052, half is due October 1 and half March 1, and unpaid halves are delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. A weekend or holiday delinquency date moves to the next business day, which is why the first half of 2026 ran through 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2. That date has passed.

  • Full-year 2026 tax over $100 can be paid without interest through December 31, 2026.
  • The second half is due March 1, 2027.
  • May 1, 2027 falls on a Saturday, so the second half becomes delinquent at 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.
  • Bills of $100 or less are due in full October 1 and delinquent after December 31.

Interest on late tax is 16% a year, simple, from the delinquency date under A.R.S. 42-18053, and no interest is charged when the full-year tax is paid by December 31 or when an assessor or treasurer error caused the delinquency. The county Treasurer's calendar also lists an advertising fee in January for delinquent taxes and an online lien auction in February.

How do you appeal a Mesa home's assessed value?

File with the Maricopa County Assessor within 60 days after the Notice of Value was mailed. The notice goes out between January 1 and March 1, and A.R.S. 42-16051 sets the 60-day window with a postmark counting as filing. The petition must state your opinion of full cash value and back it with a method such as a comparable property or a recent sale.

The Assessor's process handout says an appeal reviews the full cash value and the legal classification, not the limited property value. Limited value is the figure used for tax and is capped at 5% growth a year unless the house changes. Mesa's city page explains the lag: values rest on sales from two to three years earlier, so the value used for fiscal 2025/26 came from mid-2022 to mid-2023 sales.

If the Assessor's answer does not satisfy you, the State Board of Equalization takes an appeal within 25 days of the decision, and Superior Court tax court or small claims is open by December 15 of the notice year or within 60 days of an administrative decision. Small claims fits owner-occupied homes and property valued under $2 million. A rental house that is not the owner's primary residence goes to tax court.

What is Mesa like, and why does it matter for a sale?

Mesa is the third-largest city in Arizona, with 504,258 residents in the 2020 census and a 2025 estimate of 513,656. It covers about 139 square miles, runs roughly 18 miles from Price Road in the west to Meridian Road in the east, and was registered as a one-square-mile townsite on July 17, 1878 and incorporated in 1883. Hohokam canals came first, and Mormon settlers in 1877 and 1878 reused some of them.

Center Street divides Mesa into east and west, and the numbering system there differs from Phoenix's, so check a Mesa address carefully. The Superstition Freeway (U.S. 60), Loop 101 and Loop 202 serve the city, and Valley Metro light rail runs about four miles along Main Street. Falcon Field in the northeast and Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport in the southeast serve the area. Boeing builds the AH-64 Apache helicopter at Falcon Field, and Mesa Public Schools, Banner Health and Boeing led the city's 2022 employer list.

Most of Mesa is in Mesa Public Schools, with the south in Gilbert Public Schools, the Higley Unified School District and the Queen Creek Unified School District and a small west edge in Tempe districts. A buyer shopping by school district will ask which one covers your address, and the district also shapes the school levy on your bill.

Does Mesa's climate or age affect the tax and the sale?

Climate affects the house more than the bill. Mesa has a hot desert climate. East Mesa's July average high is 105.9 degrees, the record is 121, and annual rainfall averages 10.76 inches. Have the age of the roof and the cooling system ready when you list.

Tax exposure matters when the house has changed. New construction, additions or a change in use can lift limited property value past the 5% cap and bring a Notice of Change from the Assessor, which carries a 25-day appeal window to the State Board of Equalization. Keep permit records for additions. Mesa grew from 16,790 residents in 1950 to 63,049 in 1970 and passed 500,000 by 2020, so house ages vary widely from one neighborhood to the next.

What should a Mesa seller do about tax due at closing?

Treat the county bill as a payoff. The lien for the tax year attached on January 1 under A.R.S. 42-17153 and ranks ahead of other liens except state liens and liens for taxes of other years. Ask the Treasurer for the amount owed through your closing date, share it with the title company, and have it paid from proceeds. If a half is delinquent, interest has been running since its delinquency date.

The affidavit of property value required by A.R.S. 11-1133 goes with the deed to the Maricopa County Recorder, whose standard recording fee is $30 per document. The title company normally handles both steps.

More questions about Mesa, AZ Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Mesa charge property tax?

Yes, but only a secondary property tax. Mesa does not collect a primary property tax. The secondary tax pays voter-approved general obligation bonds, and the 2025/26 rate was $0.8582 per $100 of value, which came to $159 for the median-value Mesa home.

Who do I pay Mesa property tax to?

Pay the Maricopa County Treasurer, which bills and collects for Mesa and for the county, schools and special districts. Call 602-506-8511 or use the Treasurer's website. The Treasurer's office is at 301 West Jefferson Street, Suite 100, Phoenix, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

When was the first half of 2026 Mesa property tax delinquent?

After 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026. November 1 fell on a Sunday, so the deadline moved to the next business day. The full-year deadline to avoid interest is December 31, 2026, and the second half is due March 1, 2027.

How long do I have to appeal my Mesa property value?

You have 60 days from the date the Maricopa County Assessor mailed your Notice of Value. File a Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation with the Assessor. After that, the State Board of Equalization takes appeals within 25 days of the Assessor's decision.

Can I sell a Mesa house that has unpaid property tax?

Yes. The tax is a lien on the property, and the title company pays it from your sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff through your closing date, because interest of 16% a year applies to delinquent amounts.
